blocks.title: About this page
blocks.text: Written for this site as of November 2026 for a fresher who wants experienced-level depth, in the style of the Java Full Stack guides. Every example titled `*.py` was run when this page was built, on Python 3.12.13 with FastAPI 0.162.0, Pydantic 2.14.2, SQLAlchemy 2.1.8, Django 6.1.3, and the output shown is what it really printed. Python and its libraries change quickly (and some examples need servers that a build cannot start, so those are only syntax-checked): check the official documentation for anything newer before relying on a detail.

A **heap** is a tree stored in an array that always exposes its minimum (or maximum) in O(1) and supports push and pop in O(log n). Python's `heapq` is a **min-heap** on a plain list. Use a heap whenever the question is "give me the best element so far, repeatedly" or "keep only the k best".

**Signals.** "k largest/smallest/most frequent", "merge k sorted", "running median", "always process the smallest next" (scheduling, Dijkstra).

The top-k trick: to keep the **k largest**, hold a **min-heap of size k**. A new item beats the smallest of the current best k (`heap[0]`) or it does not; each step costs O(log k), so n items cost O(n log k), better than sorting all n.

blocks.title: Heaps.py

blocks.text: Counter-intuitive but standard: to keep the **k largest**, use a **min**-heap of size k, because its root is the *smallest of the best k*, the first thing to evict. To keep the k smallest, use a max-heap (negate values in Python). Say why; it signals you understand the structure rather than the recipe.
blocks.title: Min-heap versus max-heap for "k largest"

blocks.text:
A **graph** is nodes (vertices) and edges. Store it as an **adjacency list** (a dict from node to neighbours): O(V + E) space, the right choice for sparse graphs and what interviews expect. Many problems hide a graph: a grid (cells are nodes, moves are edges), a word list (words one letter apart), a state machine.

- **DFS** (stack or recursion) goes deep first: connectivity, cycles, components, paths, backtracking.
- **BFS** (queue) goes level by level: **shortest path in an unweighted graph**, fewest moves, nearest something.
- Always track **visited**, or a cycle makes the search run forever.

blocks.title: GraphSearch.py

blocks.text:
| Task | Algorithm | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reachable? components? | DFS or BFS with a visited set | O(V + E) |
| Fewest edges (unweighted shortest path) | **BFS** | O(V + E) |
| Cycle in an **undirected** graph | DFS, ignoring the parent edge (or union-find) | O(V + E) |
| Cycle in a **directed** graph | DFS with three colours (a back edge to a node on the current path) | O(V + E) |
| Two-colourable? | BFS/DFS colouring | O(V + E) |
| Spread from many sources at once | **Multi-source BFS** (put all sources in the queue first) | O(V + E) |

For a **directed acyclic graph** (DAG) of dependencies, a **topological order** lists every node after all nodes it depends on. It answers: "in what order can tasks run?", and fails exactly when the graph has a cycle. **Kahn's algorithm**: repeatedly remove nodes with in-degree 0.

blocks.title: Topological.py

blocks.text: **Union-find** maintains groups of elements and answers "are these two in the same group?" and "merge these two groups" in nearly constant time (with path compression and union by size). It is the tool for **dynamic connectivity** and for building minimum spanning trees with Kruskal's algorithm.

blocks.title: UnionFind.py

blocks.text:
| Situation | Algorithm | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unweighted edges | BFS | O(V + E) |
| Non-negative weights | **Dijkstra** with a min-heap | O((V + E) log V) |
| Negative weights, or a limit on the number of edges | **Bellman-Ford** | O(VE) |
| All pairs, small graphs | Floyd-Warshall | O(V³) |

**Dijkstra** repeatedly settles the unsettled node with the smallest known distance (the heap), then relaxes its edges. It is greedy and is correct only if **no edge weight is negative**.

blocks.title: ShortestPaths.py

blocks.text: Dijkstra permanently settles a node when it is popped, assuming no later path can be shorter, which holds only if adding edges never decreases a path's length. A negative edge can make a longer-looking path cheaper after the node was settled. Use Bellman-Ford (which also detects negative cycles), or reweight the graph (Johnson's algorithm).
blocks.title: Why can't Dijkstra handle negative edges?

items.question: What is the complexity of finding the k largest of n items with a heap?
items.answer: O(n log k) time and O(k) space: each of the n items is compared with the heap root and, if better, costs one push and one pop of O(log k). Sorting would be O(n log n); quickselect is O(n) on average.

items.question: How does the two-heap median finder work?
items.answer: A max-heap holds the smaller half and a min-heap the larger half, kept balanced (sizes equal or the lower one larger by one). The median is the lower root, or the mean of both roots. Insertion is O(log n), lookup O(1).

items.question: Why is `heapq.heapify` O(n) rather than O(n log n)?
items.answer: Sifting down from the middle of the array towards the root, most nodes are near the leaves and move very little; the sum of the sift-down costs over all levels converges to O(n).

items.question: Why does BFS find the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
items.answer: It explores nodes in order of increasing distance: all nodes at distance d are dequeued before any at distance d + 1, so the first time it reaches a node is along a shortest path. With weighted edges this breaks and you need Dijkstra.

items.question: How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph?
items.answer: DFS with three states: unvisited, on the current recursion path, finished. If an edge leads to a node that is on the current path, there is a cycle. (An edge to a finished node is fine.) Kahn's topological sort detects it too, by failing to remove all nodes.

items.question: What is multi-source BFS and when do you use it?
items.answer: Put all source nodes in the queue at distance 0 before starting, so the search expands from all of them simultaneously. It computes, for every cell, the distance to the nearest source in one pass (rotting oranges, walls and gates, 01-matrix).

items.question: When do you need a topological sort?
items.answer: Whenever items have dependencies and you need a valid execution order: build systems, course prerequisites, task schedulers, package installation (pip's resolver), spreadsheet cell evaluation. If the sort cannot place every node, the dependencies contain a cycle.

items.question: How does Kahn's algorithm detect a cycle?
items.answer: Nodes on a cycle never reach in-degree 0, so they are never queued. If the output contains fewer nodes than the graph, a cycle exists.

items.question: Union-find or DFS for connected components?
items.answer: For a static graph both are O(V + E). Union-find shines when edges **arrive over time** (dynamic connectivity), when you need to know whether adding an edge creates a cycle, or in Kruskal's algorithm; DFS is simpler when the graph is fully known and you also need paths.

items.question: What two optimisations make union-find fast, and what is the resulting cost?
items.answer: Union by size (attach the smaller tree to the larger) and path compression (flatten the tree during `find`). Together they give amortised O(α(n)) per operation, where α is the inverse Ackermann function, effectively constant.

items.question: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra with a binary heap?
items.answer: O((V + E) log V): each edge may push one entry (O(log V) each) and each node is settled once. The "stale entry" check (`d > dist[node]`) skips outdated heap entries instead of needing a decrease-key operation.

items.question: When do you choose BFS, Dijkstra or Bellman-Ford?
items.answer: BFS for unweighted graphs (or all weights equal), Dijkstra for non-negative weights, Bellman-Ford for negative weights or when the number of edges on the path is limited (cheapest flight with at most k stops).
